title: 8/n and k/n siblings: Kahn–Kalai threshold across the numerator k
connection: Varying the numerator k (k/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z) changes the expected solution count; Schinzel–Sierpiński-type problems are open for each k ≥ 4.
why: A threshold picture across k (where 'almost all' becomes 'all') calibrates ES's position.
first_step: Compute failure counts of k/n for k = 4..12, n ≤ 10^6 (excluding trivial obstructions) and fit expected-count vs failure-rate curves.
alt_first_steps: [free_astra-0295] Derive the residual factor equation for k=3,4,5 and compare congruence conditions for the same x ansatz.
refs: Elsholtz, Sums of k unit fractions, Trans. AMS 353 (2001)

title: Separable and inseparable parametrizations
connection: Check whether a function-field construction relies on derivatives or Frobenius powers that have no direct integer analogue.
why: Separating these mechanisms can identify the genuinely transferable algebraic part.
first_step: For a candidate polynomial parametrization, compute its derivative and determine whether its parameter map is separable.

title: Smallest-solution growth: is min_{solutions} max(x,y,z) ≤ p^{1+o(1)}?
connection: Bounds on the size of the smallest solution are a different pointwise statement than existence; the exponent governs which algorithmic approaches (Coppersmith bivariate: roots up to N^{1/3}…) could be made *provably* complete.
why: If the smallest solution has max coordinate ≈ p^{3/2} typically, then no 'small roots' method is complete; if ≈ p log p, there's hope for a lattice-based constructive proof.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁷ the smallest max-coordinate solution and fit the growth exponent; check repo for existing data (git grep -i 'smallest solution\|max(x,y,z)').

title: Zero-knowledge-style 'succinct witness' for ES(p): what is the shortest certificate as a function of p?
connection: A solution (x,y,z) is a 3·log p-bit witness; a (C, divisor) is 2·log p bits; the ES₅ CF form is ~log p + small. The minimal witness length (information-theoretically) across p is a 'compressibility of the certificate'.
why: If a witness of O(log log p) extra bits beyond p exists for every p (i.e. 'which of polylog many templates'), ES is 'almost covered' by a polylog-size list — a different proof shape than existing ones.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10⁷, the minimal index of a winning C in the ordering by C; its log is the witness length; compare growth with log log p.

title: Reed–Solomon-type interpolation: can the map p ↦ (x,y,z) be interpolated by a low-degree polynomial over a finite field F_q?
connection: Over F_q (q a prime of size ~ range), the 'first solution' map restricted to primes is a function; its degree as a polynomial over F_q (via interpolation) compared to the number of points measures 'algebraicity'.
why: If the map had degree far below the number of points for structured subsets (e.g. primes in a fixed class mod M), those subsets are covered by an algebraic rule — a new identity family.
first_step: Take primes ≡ 1 mod 840 up to 10⁵, interpolate C_min(p) mod q as a polynomial in p mod q, check the degree vs number of points; expect full degree (no structure) — a negative result calibrates B1.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Thue's lemma / Brillhart-style two-squares proof pattern applied to p² + 4c²d
connection: The two-squares theorem's elementary proofs (Thue's lemma: for a² ≡ −1 mod p find small x,y with x ≡ ay mod p) produce a divisor from a square root. Type I needs f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p mod 4cd; i.e. a 'square root of −4c²d' structure.
why: Thue's lemma is the canonical rigidity mechanism (R) that produces a pointwise divisor; the question is whether the congruence f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) can be built into the lattice.
first_step: Fix c,d; the condition is f | p² + 4c²d ⟺ p² ≡ −4c²d (mod f); if −4c²d is a QR mod f, Thue gives a representation f·k = u² + 4c²d v² with small u,v; check whether choosing f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) is compatible with the Thue box.

title: Explicit infinite family inside the square classes via Bateman–Horn-free arguments: p with 4p+1 having a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4
connection: 4p + 1 (C = 1) has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4 iff 4p+1 has a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4 (since 4p+1 ≡ 1 mod 4, it has an even number of such factors, so ≥ 2 if any; any prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4 is itself a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4). So C = 1 wins iff 4p + 1 is not a product of primes ≡ 1 mod 4 — i.e. iff 4p+1 is not a sum of two squares in the 'all factors 1 mod 4' sense.
why: This is a clean, non-polynomial criterion: ES(p) holds whenever 4p+1 is not entirely composed of primes ≡ 1 mod 4. The complementary set (4p+1 all of whose prime factors are ≡ 1 mod 4) has density → 0 (Landau–Ramanujan-type, ~ 1/√log p). Likewise C = 2: 8p+1 not all factors ≡ 1 mod 8 ... each C removes a 1/√log-density set; the intersection is the real target. Document this chain explicitly as the cleanest statement of 'why the heuristic count is log²p but no proof'.
first_step: Verify the claim (C = 1 Type II wins iff 4p+1 has a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4) against the repo's divisor form; compute the density of primes p ≤ 10⁷ with 4p+1 having only factors ≡ 1 mod 4; then for C=1..K the joint density.

title: Jacobsthal function analogue: longest run of C with 4Cp+1 'bad'
connection: The Jacobsthal function j(m) is the longest gap between integers coprime to m; here, define J(p) = C_min(p) − 1 = the longest initial run of bad C. Jacobsthal-type upper bounds (Iwaniec: j(m) ≪ log²m) are *pointwise*, proved by sieve.
why: If 'bad C' could be modelled as 'C hitting a residue class mod each small prime' (like non-coprimality), Iwaniec's method would bound C_min(p) ≪ log²p pointwise — a proof! The model is wrong (badness is not a congruence condition in C) but the degree of mismatch is the question.
first_step: Test empirically whether badness of C is 'locally determined': for fixed p, is the set of bad C periodic mod small moduli? (Compute correlation of bad(C) with C mod q.)

title: ES in ℤ/mℤ for all m (local solvability) as a finite-automaton: compute the minimal m where local information already determines 'how many lifts'
connection: Local solvability is trivial (Bright–Loughran), but the *number* of solutions mod m with lifting structure (Hensel) gives a 'local density' σ_m(p); the product over m of σ_m is the singular series. For fixed p, the singular series Π_q σ_q(p) is an explicit function of p's residues; its size vs the actual f(p) is the 'global vs local' gap.
why: Singular-series-to-actual-count ratios are informative; if f(p)/S(p) concentrates, the hard part is the archimedean/size part, not local arithmetic.
first_step: Compute S(p) = Π_{q ≤ 100} σ_q(p) with σ_q = (# solutions mod q)/q² and compare to f(p) for p ≤ 10⁵; regress.

title: Erdős–Rényi random graph threshold: at what 'connectivity' does the prime–template bipartite graph lose isolated vertices?
connection: An isolated prime (no template among those used by primes ≤ X) is a 'locally unique' solver; the growth of the number of isolated primes vs X measures the entropy of the solution structure.
why: If isolated primes vanish (every prime shares a template with another), the templates form a 'cover with reuse', a weak form of structure.
first_step: Build the bipartite graph (primes ≤ 10⁶, templates = (C, a mod 4C) or (c,d)); count isolated vertices as a function of X.

title: Analogy: Goldbach's 'every even n is p + q' vs ES's 'every p has a certificate' — the Hardy–Littlewood singular series as the ES 'local factor' and its *minimum* over p
connection: For Goldbach the singular series S(n) ≥ 1 > 0 uniformly; for ES, the analogous local product (over small primes q of the local solution density) could in principle degenerate for some p — a 'local near-obstruction' that makes certain p hard. Compute the min of S_ES(p) over p and see whether it correlates with small f(p).
why: If min_p S_ES(p) is bounded below (like Goldbach), hardness is purely 'global'; if S_ES(p) → 0 along a subsequence (near-squares?), that's a local mechanism for hard primes worth understanding.
first_step: Define S_ES(p) = Π_{q ≤ Q} (local density of (c,d,f) solutions mod q normalised); compute for p ≤ 10⁶; correlate with f(p).

title: Pure analogy: Erdős's '2^n mod n' and 'p + 2^k' problems vs ES — the 'exponential reservoir' difference
connection: Problems with reservoir 2^k (k ≤ log N: only log N candidates) are like ES (polylog candidates) and remain open (p + 2^k not covering an AP — proved by Erdős via covering congruences!). Erdős's covering construction PROVES failure of 'every odd n is p + 2^k' — a negative result via coverings. For ES, is there a covering-congruence construction showing that some explicit residue class of n has NO solution of a restricted shape (e.g. with max(x,y,z) ≤ n²)? That would be a 'restricted-ES is false' result, calibrating which restrictions are safe.
why: Erdős's covering-congruence method is the standard way to prove 'polylog-reservoir' problems FAIL on an AP; applying it to restricted versions of ES tells which restrictions (bounds on x,y,z; Type I only; d = 1 only) are provably insufficient.
first_step: Try to construct a covering of ℤ by classes n ≡ r_i (mod m_i) such that each class forces 'no Type I solution with d = 1' (via a local obstruction like T1 but for the class); if achievable, 'd = 1 Type I' is provably not a complete mechanism on an AP.

title: Analogy: Lehmer's problem on Euler's totient / 'n | 2^n − 2'-type statements and the 'divisor of a shifted multiple' structure
connection: 'a | 4Cp+1 with a ≡ −1 mod 4C' is a divisor-of-shifted-multiple condition like 'p | 2^{p−1} − 1' (Fermat) or Wieferich; in those, rigidity comes from group orders (Lagrange). Is there a group in which 4Cp+1's divisors arise as orders of elements (so Lagrange forces structure)?
why: If a | 4Cp+1 ⟺ some element has order dividing 4Cp+1 in a group of order a ... (e.g. a | 4Cp+1 ⟺ ord_a(something) | 4Cp+1); then the condition a ≡ −1 mod 4C is about a's group having an element of order a+1/(4C)... Speculative, but 'orders of elements in (ℤ/a)^×' is rigid.
first_step: Note that a | 4Cp+1 ⟺ 4Cp ≡ −1 mod a ⟺ (4C)·p ≡ −1: p ≡ −(4C)^{−1}; no group-order content. Drop unless a different group (e.g. elliptic curve over F_a with a + 1 − t points) gives a + 1 = 4C·(…) — Hasse's theorem: #E(F_a) = a + 1 − t; if #E = a + 1 (supersingular, t = 0) then 4C | #E(F_a) is a condition on the curve, and 'a ≡ −1 mod 4C' ⟺ 4C | a + 1 = #E for supersingular E. Interesting: certificates ⟺ supersingular curves over F_a with 4C | #E and a | 4Cp+1.

title: Analogy: Zsigmondy/Bang — every a^n − 1 has a primitive prime divisor (n > 6) — a pointwise 'new divisor exists' theorem; its mechanism (cyclotomic factorisation + size) for 4Cp+1?
connection: Bang–Zsigmondy proves existence of a divisor with a prescribed property (primitive) for EVERY n by exhibiting a factor Φ_n(a) that is large and whose prime factors are ≡ 1 mod n (rigid congruence from cyclotomic theory). ES wants a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C of 4Cp+1. Is there a polynomial identity 4Cp+1 = (algebraic factor) with controlled residues when p itself has a special form (p = Φ_m(a)-ish)? For p of the form (a^m − 1)/(a − 1) or similar, 4Cp+1 might factor cyclotomically for suitable C — giving ES for 'repunit-like' primes unconditionally.
why: Would give explicit infinite families (conditional on infinitely many such primes — which is itself open for repunits), but the mechanism (cyclotomic rigidity) is one of the two accepted (R) mechanisms.
first_step: For p = (a^m − 1)/(a − 1) (prime), search small C with 4Cp+1 factoring as a product of cyclotomic-like polynomials in a; e.g. a = 2: p = 2^m − 1 (Mersenne, ≡ 3 mod 4 — easy class!). Try a = 4, 10, and p = a^m + 1 forms.

title: abc-conjecture consequences: does abc bound the size of the smallest certificate or forbid 'all 4Cp+1 nearly prime for C ≤ K'?
connection: abc gives bounds on smooth/powerful values of polynomials; the 'hard prime' heuristic requires 4Cp+1 to be nearly prime (few factors) for all small C — not an abc-type condition. But abc does bound solutions of, e.g., 4Cp + 1 = a·b with a, b both powerful; not relevant. Mostly a negative: abc is about radicals, ES about residues. Keep as a 5-minute check.
why: Rule out quickly; conditional abc results are popular and someone will ask.
first_step: Write one paragraph: why abc (radical-based) is orthogonal to residue-class divisor conditions; note any exception (e.g. Granville's 'abc ⟹ squarefree values of polynomials' would make 4Cp+1 squarefree often — mild help for the subset-product counting).
refs: Granville, 'ABC allows us to count squarefrees' (1998)

title: Catalan/Mihăilescu-style cyclotomic rigidity for 'ab = 4Cp+1, a + 1 ≡ b + 1 ≡ 0 mod 4C': a Wieferich-type congruence?
connection: Mihăilescu's proof of Catalan used Wieferich-type pairs (p^{q−1} ≡ 1 mod q²) derived from cyclotomic unit structure. The ES C-form has the structure ab ≡ 1 (mod p) with a ≡ b ≡ −1 (mod 4C) and 4C | (ab − 1)/p... Any 'double congruence' (mod p and mod 4C simultaneously, with 4C | ab − 1 too) resembles Wieferich conditions. Check: is ab ≡ 1 mod 4Cp? ab = 4Cp + 1 ≡ 1 mod 4Cp — yes trivially. And a ≡ −1 mod 4C ⟹ a^2 ≡ 1 mod 4C... So a² ≡ 1 (mod 4C) and ab ≡ 1 (mod 4C) ⟹ b ≡ a mod 4C ✓. Nothing deep; drop unless a cyclotomic-unit argument appears.
why: Low; included for completeness of the 'rigidity mechanisms' sweep.
first_step: Drop after noting.

title: Erdős–Straus over number fields (Gaussian, Eisenstein) with sign/positivity conditions
connection: Generalise ES to totally positive elements in totally real fields ↔ ℤ[√2], ℚ(√5).
why: In ℚ(√5) the unit group is infinite and positive; the existence of units might act as a thick reservoir that ℤ lacks, giving a proved sibling.
first_step: Brute-force 4/π = sum of three totally positive unit-reciprocals for small totally positive primes π of ℤ[(1+√5)/2]; check for failures.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0052] Compute, for K = ℚ(√2), totally positive prime elements π of norm ≤ 10⁴ and search for 4/π = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ≫ 0; look for failures.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Fermat's two-squares via Zagier's one-sentence involution and its ES analogue
connection: Zagier's involution on {x²+4yz=p} has one fixed point so the other involution has one too ↔ ES windmills (INVOLUTION_ES2).
why: Already studied; remains the canonical (T)×parity cell. Listing for completeness and to try non-affine menus.
first_step: Search for a restricted ES subset (e.g. solutions with x minimal in its Vieta orbit) whose count parity is constant on hard primes ≤ 10⁵.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0026] Enumerate solutions of 4/p in some normalised parametrisation and look for any involution whose fixed-point count is odd for all p ≤ 10⁵.
[signature-0131] Write the Zagier involution on the relevant finite representation set and test whether ES divisors d and complementary divisors can be paired without fixed points.

title: Thue's lemma / pigeonhole for x ≡ ay mod p with small x, y and ES
connection: Thue: for any a there exist |x|,|y| ≤ √p with x ≡ ay (mod p) ↔ ES Type II pair form p ≡ −(u+B) mod 4uB.
why: Thue is the prototypical pointwise size-squeeze; Fermat two squares follows. Is there a Thue-type statement with a modulus depending on the variables?
first_step: Search for a fixed modulus M(p) and a residue a(p) such that a small solution of x ≡ a·y mod M yields an ES certificate; test numerically for p ≤ 10⁴.

title: CRT-construction of adversarial p evading all small certificates (Chinese remainder adversary)
connection: Choose p mod Π(4uC−1) avoiding −u for all small (u,C) ↔ B1 barrier; the smallest such p as function of the menu bound.
why: Gives the 'cost' of evading menu of size B; growth rate of the minimal evader vs actual certificate sizes calibrates how big the menu must be at p.
first_step: Compute minimal prime p ≡ 1 mod 840 avoiding all (u,C) with 4uC−1 ≤ B for B = 10..200 via CRT + sieve; plot log p vs B.

title: Chen's theorem analogue: 4Cp+1 is P₂ for some small C
connection: Chen-type: for each p, some 4Cp+1 with C ≤ polylog is a product of ≤ 2 primes? ↔ unproven at fixed p; Chen is about averages over p.
why: Calibration: shows even 'some 4Cp+1 has a specific factorisation shape' at fixed p is out of reach of sieves — ES needs such fixed-p statements.
first_step: Record as barrier-calibration: list fixed-p statements about {4Cp+1 : C ≤ (log p)^A} that are known (e.g. not all prime? trivially: some is divisible by 3) and the strongest such.

title: Bateman–Horn densities for primes in hard families as test of B1-type evasion
connection: Bateman–Horn predicts counts of primes in polynomial families ↔ quantify how many primes in a family each certificate class covers.
why: Calibration for which polynomial families are ES-hardest.
first_step: For families f(m) = am² + bm + c generating primes ≡ 1 mod 840, compute average R(f(m))/M; find hardest family.

title: I3 extremal function: least u over primes, as a 'Jacobsthal function' analogue
connection: Least certifying interior endpoint u(p) ≤ 39 to 10⁹ ↔ Jacobsthal function j(m) (max gap in integers coprime to m) controls CRT evasions.
why: Jacobsthal bounds (Iwaniec: j(m) ≪ (log m)²) are pointwise results on CRT-evasion lengths — exactly the B1 cost question; growth of max u(p) should be compared with Jacobsthal-type predictions.
first_step: Model: to evade u ≤ U requires p avoiding certain classes mod moduli depending on u; compute the 'Jacobsthal-type' minimal evader size and compare with observed max u = 39 at 10⁹.

title: Meta: 'analogy of analogies' — map ES to problems that were mapped to something solved
connection: A ↔ B ↔ C chains: ES ↔ three cubes ↔ (Heath-Brown) density heuristics; ES ↔ Markoff ↔ Chen's theorem; ES ↔ HKRS ↔ Rickards–Stange.
why: Second-order analogies sometimes connect to solved problems not linked directly.
first_step: For each first-order analogue in repo's B2_ACROSS_FIELDS.md, list its own known analogues and check whether any of those is solved with a transferable method.

title: Waring-type problems in finite groups: −1 as a product of elements from a set
connection: Waring problems in groups (every element is a product of k elements from a conjugacy class) ↔ −1 as subproduct.
why: Abelian case reduces to zero-sum; noted for completeness.
first_step: Merge with zero-sum items; no separate step (check abelian Waring results for subset products).

title: B=1 slice of (★) ⟺ (p+1)/2 has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) — a Landau–Ramanujan event
connection: B = 1 slice: need divisor s ≡ −1 mod 4 of p + 1 with s ≥ 3 ↔ p + 1 = 2·odd; odd part has a divisor ≡ 3 mod 4 iff odd part has a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4 … at an odd power? (product of primes ≡ 1 mod 4 gives ≡ 1).
why: Exact criterion: B=1 slice succeeds iff (p+1)/2 is not a product of primes ≡ 1 mod 4 (i.e. not a sum-of-two-squares-ish with only 1 mod 4 primes). Fails with density ~ c/√log p (Landau) — so B=1 alone handles all but a (log p)^{-1/2} fraction. Simple and illustrative.
first_step: CHECKED (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check2.py): criterion exact for all 8977 primes p ≡ 1 (4) below 2·10⁵; B=1 fails for 13.6% of them. Next: fit the failure fraction against c/√(log p) (Landau–Ramanujan) up to 10⁹.

title: Iterated Landau–Ramanujan: B-slice fails iff all prime factors of (p+B) avoid a set of classes mod 4B — a 'multiplicatively constrained' integer
connection: Generalising: slice B fails iff the subgroup/subset-product structure of prime factors of p+B avoids −1 mod 4B ↔ for B where (ℤ/4B)^× has a quadratic character separating −1, failure ⟸ all prime factors in its kernel: Landau–Ramanujan-type density (log)^{−1/2}.
why: Each slice fails with probability ~ (log p)^{−δ_B}; joint failure of K slices ~ product if independent — gives a clean heuristic exponent for 'K slices all fail' and connects to sieve dimension.
first_step: Compute δ_B (the density exponent of slice-failure) for B ≤ 30 theoretically (via Chebotarev in (ℤ/4B)^×) and compare with data.

title: Covering-radius analogy: CRT evasion as covering radius of a 'certificate code'
connection: Residue classes avoided by an adversarial p ↔ a word at maximal distance from a code; B1 = covering radius > 0 for any finite code.
why: Coding theory has tight covering-radius bounds; might quantify 'how many certificate classes needed to cover primes ≤ X' as a function of X.
first_step: Define code C_B = set of certificate class vectors for moduli ≤ B; compute empirically the fraction of residue vectors not covered as B grows (ties to set-cover item).

title: Chebyshev-bias analogue: are certain classes mod 840·k systematically harder?
connection: Prime number races / Chebyshev bias ↔ per-class average of R(p)/M(p) among the six Mordell-hard classes mod 840 and their lifts.
why: Systematic class biases indicate local factors not yet in M_BM — refinement of the main term or new local invariant.
first_step: Compute mean R(p)/M_BM(p) per class mod 840·11·13 for primes ≤ 10⁸ and test for significant deviations.

title: Sibling: n = xyz − x − y − z (and n = xyz − x − y) universality thresholds
connection: I3: n = tuv − u − v with t,u,v ≥ 3 covers all n > 2 433 600 ↔ sibling shapes xyz − x − y − z, xyz + x + y may have their own exception lists and known proofs.
why: Sibling exception structures calibrate I3_𝒞 (repo's ES-strength conjecture); a sibling with a provable finite exception list would be a method precedent.
first_step: Compute exceptions of n = xyz − x − y − z with x,y,z ≥ 2 up to 10⁷; inspect whether the exception set is finite-looking and whether it has a T1-like obstruction (squares?).

title: Feature flip: fixed small t — t ≤ 3 is trivially universal on odd n, fixed t = 4 has a primality-type failure set
connection: The word tuv − u − v with u = 1 gives (t−1)v − 1, so t = 2 or 3 (and t = 1, = Frobenius numbers g(u,v) = uv−u−v, e.g. g(2,n+2) = n) represents every odd n trivially. Fixed t = 4 gives n = 4uv − u − v ⟺ 4n+1 = (4u−1)(4v−1), which fails e.g. whenever 4n+1 is prime. ES needs the union over t ∈ 4ℤ (plus the glued third generator u+v in the semigroup picture).
why: Shows precisely which features (t restricted to 4ℤ, union over levels) turn a trivial or primality-type single-level statement into a plausible universality statement.
first_step: Tabulate which odd n (and primes) fail to be 4Cuv − u − v for each fixed C = 1,2,3,… separately (each level has its own divisor-type failure set) and for unions over C ≤ K.

title: Least quadratic non-residue: exists iff n is not a square — the exact reciprocity shape of T1
connection: For n > 1, some prime ℓ has (n/ℓ) = −1 iff n is not a square; the least one is ≪ log²n under GRH (Ankeny/Bach) and ≪ n^{1/(4√e)+ε} unconditionally. ES's BM layer is pointwise free iff n is not a square (SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9 Prop 2.2).
why: This is the only fully solved problem whose failure set is exactly the squares; ES's remaining difficulty is the 'one more character' step beyond it.
first_step: Quantify: for hard primes ≤ 10⁹ correlate ℓ(p) (least non-residue) with R(p) and with the smallest working level; check whether R(p) is small exactly when ℓ(p) is large.

title: Goldbach–Linnik: even n = p + q + K powers of 2 (K = 8, Pintz–Ruzsa) — adding a sparse structured set makes pointwise possible
connection: Linnik showed finitely many powers of 2 suffice; Heath-Brown–Puchta K = 13, Pintz–Ruzsa K = 8. Shares F01, F05 (binary Goldbach exceptional set) and the strategy 'almost-all + a sparse absorbing set'.
why: ES analogue: show 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z + (sum of K unit fractions from a sparse set S) with K bounded, then try to shrink K — a ladder of weakenings with K = ∞ trivial.
first_step: Define ES_K(S): 4/p − Σ_{i≤K} 1/s_i ∈ {1/x+1/y+1/z} for some s_i ∈ S = {2^j}; compute the least K needed for p ≤ 10⁷.
refs: unverified: Heath-Brown, Puchta 2002, Integers represented as a sum of primes and powers of two (Asian J. Math.)

title: Crocker: infinitely many odd n ≠ p + 2^a + 2^b — polylog expected count yet infinitely many failures
connection: Expected count ≍ log n (polylog), like ES, but Crocker exhibits infinitely many exceptions. Shares F04, F24w.
why: Key calibration: a polylog expected count alone does not imply finitely many failures. Learn what structure Crocker's exceptions exploit and check that ES cannot be attacked the same way.
first_step: Check whether Crocker's exceptions come from a covering-type construction (e.g. n = 2^{2^m} − 1) and whether an ES analogue (n in a sparse algebraic family) has abnormally small R(n).
refs: unverified: Crocker 1971, On the sum of a prime and of two powers of two (Pacific J. Math.)

title: Borwein conjecture (Chen Wang, Adv. Math. 2022): sign pattern of q-product coefficients by saddle-point + finite check
connection: ES ⟺ positivity/nonvanishing of coefficients of an explicit theta-quotient level series at prime indices (F19). Wang proved a coefficient sign pattern for all n analytically.
why: Feature flip: Wang's coefficients have an exponentially dominant main term; ES's are divisor-sized. Clarifies that an ES q-series proof needs a positivity mechanism, not asymptotics.
first_step: Look for a manifestly positive (product/sum-of-squares) expression of Σ_n R(n)q^n restricted to a progression, e.g. via Andrews-style identities.

title: Continuants: p = K(a,b,c) = abc + a + c (positive CF) vs ES's negative continuant tuv − u − v
connection: Length-3 continuants K(a,b,c) = abc + a + c represent every n > ? trivially (a = c = 1: b + 2), while the negative-CF version with a 4ℤ constraint is ES. The sign flip is the feature (F16, F27).
why: The positive version is trivially universal; ES lives exactly between positive and negative continuants — a mixed-sign continuant 'abc + a − c' family may interpolate.
first_step: For the 4 sign patterns of abc ± a ± c with a 4ℤ constraint on one coordinate, compute failure sets among primes ≤ 10⁷.

title: Feature flip F28: forbid Type I (p | exactly one denominator) — Type II alone fails at 14+ primes; union never fails ≤ 10⁸
connection: Restricting the type creates explicit failure sets ((★) fails at 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰; b = 1 line at 3 primes ≤ 10¹¹); their union survives. Shares the 'two families, each with sparse failures, disjoint failure sets' structure with Heath-Brown's Artin and with Goldbach-type unions.
why: If failure sets of two families can be shown disjoint by a parity/sign argument (one fails ⇒ the other has many), ES follows for large p.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁹ the joint distribution of (R_(★)(p), R_{b=1}(p)) and test for negative correlation at small values.

title: Feature flip F02: problems without multiplicative closure (Goldbach) can't reduce to primes — ES's prime reduction as an asset
connection: ES(n) ⇐ ES(d) for d | n reduces to primes; for primes the multiplicative structure of n is gone. Conversely, composites have MORE solutions (Elsholtz–Planitzer).
why: Suggests 'prime-free' proofs: use auxiliary composites m = p·k with ES(pk) solutions having k | all denominators (equivalent to ES(p)).
first_step: For hard p, find the smallest k such that 4/(pk) has a solution with k dividing all three denominators — equals ES(p) — but study the distribution of 'near-misses' (k dividing two denominators).

title: Feature flip F21: problems where a pointwise bound came from averaging over an auxiliary parameter of length ≫ polylog
connection: Pointwise results (Linnik p + x² + y², Vinogradov three primes, Duke ternary) all average over an auxiliary variable of polynomial length. ES's auxiliary variables (C, u, B) have polynomial range but polylog effective mass.
why: Suggests looking for an ES formulation with an auxiliary average of polynomial MASS (e.g. counting weighted solutions with weights growing in C).
first_step: Search for a weighting w(C,u,B) with Σ w·1[event] provably positive and mass ≫ p^δ — e.g. weights from smooth-number counts.

title: Feature flip F17: CF length ≤ 2 — which primes are length-2 (two-term) representable — fully explicit
connection: λ(p) ≤ 2 corresponds to 2-term-type representations, characterised by divisor conditions (Rav). ES₅ is the length-3 rung.
why: Explicit rung below ES; the step 2 → 3 adds one free parameter, which is where the log² count appears.
first_step: Compute the density of primes with λ(p) ≤ 2 (under ES₅ constraints) — should decay like a power of 1/log.

title: Precedent search: theorems giving r(n) ≫ (log n)^c for ALL n (polylog pointwise lower bounds)
connection: Examples to check: number of prime factors-related counts, r(n) for sums of a prime and a square-free?, number of divisors in a dense set; the 'every n has ≫ log n representations as p + 2^a + 2^b' type (false). F04 + F21.
why: If no natural polylog-scale pointwise lower bound has ever been proved, ES's required statement is unprecedented — a strong strategic datum.
first_step: Ask MathOverflow-style search: 'every integer has at least log n representations'; check Erdős–Fuchs-type and additive-basis-order results.

title: Feature flip F35: problems where bounded certificate schemes DO work (Pratt certificates for primality) vs ES's B1
connection: Primality has short certificates (Pratt) found by structured search, but no bounded formula; ES has short certificates (F32) and B1 forbids bounded procedures under Schinzel H.
why: Pratt-style recursive certificates (certificate for p uses certificates for factors of p−1) suggest recursive ES certificates using solutions for factors of 4Cp+1 or p+4d.
first_step: Check whether an ES solution for p can be assembled from ES-like data for prime factors of 4Cp+1 (recursive certificate).

title: Hardy–Littlewood Conjecture H (large non-square n = p + k²) / Bateman–Horn: singular series with Legendre-symbol factors
connection: Representation counts whose singular series involve (n/ℓ) — e.g. HL Conjecture H, where squares n are excluded (n − k² factors). ES's main term M_BM has the same Legendre-symbol structure and also degenerates at squares (F20, F08).
why: Lets ES borrow the full Bateman–Horn singular-series machinery for its main term, and the known numerics for its variance.
first_step: Compare M_BM(p)/M₀(p) with a Bateman–Horn-type product ∏(1 − (p/ℓ)/(ℓ−1)) — is it asymptotically such a product?

title: Zsigmondy's theorem and its finite exceptional list
connection: Every n>1 has a new prime divisor in a cyclotomic difference except explicit small cases (F01,F23); cyclotomic factorization gives a short witness (F32) and finite exceptions (F25).
why: This is a clean example where primitive-divisor algebra turns universal existence into a finite exceptional classification.
first_step: Check whether any ES parametrization yields a cyclotomic factor whose primitive divisor forces d≡−1 mod 4C; begin with 4Cp+1.
refs: unverified: Zsigmondy, Zur Theorie der Potenzreste (1892); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zsigmondy%27s_theorem

title: Chen Wang's proof of Borwein's coefficient-positivity conjecture
connection: A coefficient-nonvanishing/positivity problem in q-series is close to ES's theta-quotient coefficient criterion (F19), while requiring control at each index (F01,F21).
why: A successful q-series positivity method could directly inform the ES coefficient lens rather than merely its Diophantine parametrizations.
first_step: Fetch Wang's paper; extract the coefficient recurrence/positivity mechanism and test the first recurrence terms of ES's generating function.
refs: https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.10886 (Chen Wang, An analytic proof of the Borwein Conjecture)

title: Finite congruence obstruction tests for universal forms
connection: Local representability is checked prime-by-prime, then a finite criterion can settle universality (F01,F03,F06); ES also has a finite congruence cover but no global witness criterion.
why: It suggests auditing whether ES's known finite modular cover can be strengthened by a local-to-global theorem on the corresponding family of forms.
first_step: For each ES residue class modulo 840, compute the local densities of the associated ternary form and test whether a finite criterion set can control all classes.

title: Conditional Artin proof versus ES's missing pointwise lower bound
connection: Hooley's conditional result combines a pointwise target with GRH-controlled character sums and a sieve (F20,F21,F22); ES shares the character-sum/sieve signature but lacks its proven lower bound (F36).
why: This is a direct diagnostic comparison of which analytic input turns a character average into strict positivity.
first_step: Map every Hooley error term to an ES analogue in R(p)=Σ_C #{d|4Cp+1:d≡−1 mod 4C}; identify the single term preventing positivity.
refs: C. Hooley, On Artin's conjecture, J. reine angew. Math. 225 (1967) 209–220 (http://eudml.org/doc/150785)

title: Least-nonresidue square failure as ES feature flip
connection: Least quadratic nonresidue existence is pointwise away from squares, while squares are exactly where the quadratic character degenerates (F01,F08w). This feature flip isolates a natural thin exceptional set rather than an analytic failure.
why: ES's square-class failures might similarly come from a character becoming principal, suggesting a decomposition by square-free kernel before applying character bounds.
first_step: Compute the real-character contribution to R(p) separately on p's square classes and test for an analogue of the principal-character degeneration.
refs: D. A. Burgess, The distribution of quadratic residues and non-residues, Mathematika 4 (1957) 106–112

title: Weak approximation versus actual ES witnesses
connection: arXiv:2411.02629 analyzes weak and strong approximation alongside semi-integral Hasse principles for Markoff orbifold pairs; this matches ES F06/F07 and F13, while highlighting the gap between local points and positive integral witnesses (F27).
why: Its separation of approximation properties from Hasse existence is relevant to avoiding a false inference from local solubility to ES solutions.
first_step: Identify the paper's examples where approximation holds or fails and translate the obstruction mechanism to the fixed-n ES surface, keeping positivity explicit.

title: Approximation off a finite set and ES residue families
connection: The strong-approximation results for Markoff orbifold pairs in arXiv:2411.02629 connect ES F06/F07/F13 with F03's congruence coverage: local approximation data may suggest congruence-class subfamilies, though not itself guarantee integral points.
why: The paper treats the interaction of local conditions and global integral-type points on a surface, providing a precise model for organizing ES congruence tests.
first_step: Extract its local-place conditions and test whether analogous conditions on ES denominator triples reproduce known Mordell classes modulo 840.

title: Zariski density is not an ES existence theorem
connection: arXiv:2504.10992 gives Markoff-type K3 surfaces with dense rational points but integral Hasse failure, matching ES F13 and contrasting F01/F07; it is a feature-flip from rational abundance to integral scarcity.
why: The distinction helps evaluate whether an ES surface argument controls integral coordinates rather than merely producing rational points.
first_step: Take one explicit surface from the paper and trace a dense rational orbit's denominators; compare with ES's reciprocal-variable divisibility requirement.

title: Near-miss identities as an ES obstruction detector
connection: ArXiv:2104.08798 studies near-miss identities for ternary integral quadratic forms under congruence conditions, matching ES F03/F21/F31 and the exceptional-set theme F25.
why: Near-miss representation identities may explain why a quadratic-form proxy succeeds for most classes but leaves stubborn exceptions.
first_step: Extract one near-miss identity and see whether an ES quadratic-form reformulation admits an analogous identity with an explicit residual term.

title: Continuant recurrences as bounded ES word identities
connection: Arxiv:2501.06512 derives a continuant formulation for second-order recurrences and associated identities, matching ES F16/F17/F19 and F32's short certificate theme.
why: Its recurrence-to-continuant translation may offer a systematic way to generate and verify short ES word identities.
first_step: Extract the recurrence identity and check whether the ES trilinear polynomial is a specialization of a continuant recurrence or determinant expansion.

title: Stern-sequence extremals and witness-count analogies
connection: Arxiv:1608.08322 proves results on largest values in Stern rows using alternating binary expansions and continuants; it matches ES F16/F17/F32 and offers a structured-word counting analogue for F04.
why: Its ordering argument is an explicit model for controlling extremal values among many short representations, not a generic heuristic.
first_step: Read its reduction of ordering to continuants and test whether the same normalization orders ES certificates for a fixed prime by denominator size.

title: Positive solution orbits versus positivity in ES
connection: The positive-integer Markov–Hurwitz solution study in arXiv:2605.05075 matches ES F01/F13/F27 and F38, where positivity is part of the arithmetic orbit structure.
why: It gives a concrete comparison for whether involutions preserve the positive cone or require discarding signed solutions.
first_step: Inspect the orbit-generation recurrence and check whether an ES analogue preserves all denominator positivity constraints.

title: Problem 305: prime-target Egyptian fraction bounds
connection: Problem 305 ↔ ES F04, F12, F21, F29: prime-specific reciprocal representations and a pointwise existence/count problem.
why: The page records the upper bounds of Bleicher–Erdős, Yokota and Liu–Sawhney for general b. For prime b it records only the lower bound D(p) ≫ p log p, so it has no prime-specific construction. Check whether the upper-bound constructions behave differently at prime denominators.
first_step: Read Yokota [Yo88] and Liu–Sawhney [LiSa24] from the page; check whether their constructions treat prime b specially, and test the construction at targets 4/p.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0239] Check whether the Bleicher–Erdős lower-bound argument for primes or the Yokota/Liu–Sawhney upper bounds distinguish p mod 4; if so, try adapting the hardest residue case to 4/p.

title: Problem 825: prime-factor threshold as feature flip
connection: Problem 825 ↔ ES features F01, F10, F12, with the flip being an imposed prime-factor restriction absent in ES.
why: The threshold theorem succeeds after restricting prime factors, highlighting whether ES can find a useful restricted subfamily of p-tied integers without losing coverage.
first_step: Read the theorem’s exact restriction in Larsen’s paper; enumerate which factorization conditions are compatible with 4Cp+1 and an ES divisor certificate.

title: Problem 308: threshold versus individual target
connection: Problem 308 ↔ ES F01, F04, F12; feature flip F01: eventual threshold statement rather than all n.
why: Croot's result shows that for large N every integer up to about H_N − (9/2+o(1))(log log N)²/log N is a sum of distinct 1/n with n ≤ N, and that this fails a little below H_N. Isolating this threshold mechanism may suggest how to handle finite exceptional sets in ES.
first_step: Read [Cr99] and identify how the least missed integer is bounded; test whether the argument yields a threshold for residual targets after one ES term.

title: Problem 316: explicit minimal obstruction and feature flip
connection: Problem 316 ↔ ES F03, F10, F12; feature flip: a finite divisor-set obstruction versus ES’s universal prime family.
why: A concrete minimal counterexample shows exactly how a divisor structure can defeat a reciprocal partition, suggesting explicit obstruction searches for ES parametrizations.
first_step: Check the cited minimal set and compute which congruence classes its divisors occupy; compare with the ES divisor-class criterion.

title: Square-factor saturation for the trilinear form xy+yz+zx
connection: OEIS A025052 studies positive integers omitted by xy+yz+zx; the page records Borwein–Choi's theorem that every N with a square factor is represented except 4 and 18. This shares F01/F08w/F13/F16w: a universal representation problem, algebraic exceptional strata, and a cubic/trilinear polynomial encoding.
why: The explicit parametrization by square-factor decomposition could suggest a way to make ES certificates from a repeated factor, distinct from residue covering.
first_step: Translate the A025052 square-factor parametrization to ES: fix n=m r² and test whether the induced denominators can be made positive integers; enumerate small m,r and record exactly where integrality fails.

title: Four-term ES decompositions as a triviality control
connection: The MathOverflow question on ES with four terms supplies a direct neighboring problem where term count changes, matching F12/F11/F32 and flipping the conjectural three-term bound to four terms.
why: A four-term baseline can validate enumeration and expose whether a proposed three-term construction loses only one controlled denominator or relies on a genuinely deep coincidence.
first_step: Implement a canonical greedy four-term decomposition for 4/p, then compare its denominator scale and residues with the shortest three-term witnesses for the same primes.

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz proof on prime-sized cyclic seats
connection: A005097's comments cite Kohen–Sadofschi: a prescribed-distance seating problem on 2n+1 seats is solvable for every distance list iff 2n+1 is prime, proved using the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz. It shares F01/F03/F29/F31: universal finite-field conditions, prime residue structure, and an algebraic certificate.
why: This is a feature-flip: universality holds precisely on primes, rather than for every integer, and the proof is polynomial nonvanishing over a finite field.
first_step: Read Kohen's Nullstellensatz argument and test whether the polynomial coefficient-extraction method yields a nonzero count for ES witnesses modulo p, especially in the difficult p≡1 mod 4 class.

title: A prime criterion hidden in a missing-value sequence
connection: A005097 is simultaneously a prime transform and a complement of a polynomial value set. It shares F10/F16w/F24/F25: one can enumerate witnesses by factor pairs and the nonrepresented values have an exact, computable criterion.
why: It shows how an apparent open-ended omission problem can collapse to a sharp criterion; search for an analogous characterization of any ES subfamily's omitted primes.
first_step: Select a natural ES subfamily (e.g. one denominator divisible by p), calculate its omitted primes, and check whether omission is equivalent to primality of a low-degree transform.

title: Residue restriction on exceptional additive representations
connection: A060003 notes that its terms greater than 3 all lie in 6n−1. This shares F03/F25/F29: congruence restrictions sharply constrain the exceptional set, while leaving a sparse residue class to investigate.
why: The exceptional set's congruence compression is an inexpensive analogue of ES square-class residue analysis, and can guide targeted rather than blind searches.
first_step: Compute ES witness counts by residue class modulo 840 and by prime splitting in Q(i), then check whether any analogous single congruence class carries almost all low-count primes.

title: Square-factor theorem as a route from a thin stratum to near-universality
connection: A025052's Borwein–Choi result covers all N with a square factor except 4,18, leaving squarefree inputs as the difficult stratum. It shares F01/F05/F08w/F25 and is a feature-flip: broad coverage is proved off the squarefree locus.
why: This is a useful structural decomposition template: establish a broad algebraic subfamily first and isolate the genuinely hard inputs explicitly.
first_step: Partition ES primes and general n by square factors in the tied divisor quantities (4Cp+1 or p+4d), and test whether the certificate family handles all but a squarefree residual condition.

title: Exceptional small values in a square-factor covering theorem
connection: The square-factor theorem for xy+yz+zx has the explicit exceptions 4 and 18. This shares F08w/F25/F27: a universal positivity-constrained representation has algebraic-family exceptions, and positivity matters to the theorem.
why: The exceptional small values may be artifacts of positivity or low-parameter degeneracy, distinctions also relevant to ES denominator positivity.
first_step: In ES parameter identities, list every boundary case where a denominator is zero, negative, or repeated; compare whether the remaining failures are similarly confined to low parameter values.

title: Collatz feature flip: almost-all control is not pointwise control
connection: Tao’s Collatz result shares ES’s universal target, computational verification, and a structured arithmetic map (F01,F23,F16w), but proves an almost-all weakened conclusion rather than all inputs (F05).
why: A feature-flip reminder: average-orbit control can coexist with unresolved exceptional inputs; it motivates studying ES exceptions structurally rather than inferring pointwise truth from density.
first_step: Check Tao’s theorem’s exact exceptional notion and test whether ES exceptional primes can be grouped by a corresponding large-deviation statistic.

title: Lonely runner: finite-dimensional torus avoidance
connection: Lonely runner shares F01, F06, F23, F24: a universal integer-speed assertion has no simple local obstruction, strong finite verification, and geometric/torus heuristics. ES similarly combines local solubility with a global integral point question (F06,F07).
why: Its reduction to simultaneous fractional-part inequalities may offer a model for separating local admissibility from global witness existence.
first_step: Read Perarnau’s survey and identify a solved small-runner argument using a finite covering of the torus; translate the covering step into ES residue classes.
refs: https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.20160 (Perarnau–Serra, The Lonely Runner Conjecture turns 60)

title: Lonely runner: cyclic gap and symmetry reduction
connection: The lonely-runner problem shares F14,F23,F24,F01 through interchangeable runner labels, finite verified cases, and a universal conjecture. ES witness permutation symmetry is S₃ (F14), likewise reducing redundant cases.
why: A careful orbit/stabilizer reduction can make exhaustive searches over ES witnesses or residue configurations substantially smaller.
first_step: Inspect the survey’s symmetry reductions and implement canonical representatives for ES triples (x,y,z) and the corresponding residue constraints.

title: EFL: approximate coloring plus absorbing reservoir
connection: EFL’s proof shares F01,F03,F05w: universal coverage is achieved by a global bound, finite local compatibility, and an absorption step. ES’s finite congruence covering and exceptional square classes have the same cover-then-patch outline (F03,F08).
why: It provides a concrete proof architecture to test: cover almost all classes cheaply, then reserve flexible certificates to repair the remainder.
first_step: Extract the EFL approximate-decomposition/absorption interface and test a toy version on ES residue classes modulo 840 with square classes left uncovered.

title: EFL feature flip: hypergraph structure versus arithmetic family
connection: EFL shares ES’s universal quantifier, finite local constraints, and proof-by-cover-plus-repair (F01,F03,F34), but its objects have a finite hypergraph decomposition while ES ranges over primes with multiplicative arithmetic (F33).
why: This feature flip identifies absorption as potentially portable only after finding an arithmetic analogue of the hypergraph reservoir.
first_step: Check whether ES certificate lines admit a bounded-overlap notion analogous to edge-disjoint color classes, then assess if an absorber can be defined.

title: Apollonian local-global feature flip: exceptional algebraic families
connection: Apollonian curvature results share ES’s local congruence restrictions, thin witnesses, and almost-all progress (F03,F05,F22), but explicit algebraic families can be missed, unlike a universal existential target. This is a feature-flip warning about exceptional subfamilies.
why: Testing for structured infinite exception families is more informative than only checking random integers.
first_step: Read the counterexample-family discussion in the 2024 paper and compare its quadratic/quartic obstructions with ES’s square-class obstruction.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0351] Read the 2024 paper’s missed-family construction and try to formulate an invariant on ES’s quadratic witness equation that vanishes on squares.

title: Ringel’s tree packing: complementarity and finite obstruction checks
connection: Ringel's conjecture (proved for large n by Montgomery–Pokrovskiy–Sudakov and Keevash–Staden) and the open graceful-tree problem share F01,F23,F34: universal finite-structure coverage, computation, and families whose union must cover all edges/labels. ES similarly unions thin prime-covering families.
why: Complementary decompositions may inspire pairing ES certificate families so their uncovered sets cancel or shrink systematically.
first_step: Identify the smallest uncovered residue class after a standard ES covering and see if a complementary parametrized line covers it.

title: Erdős–Faber–Lovász: finite colorings as congruence coverings
connection: EFL shares F01,F03,F34: every finite input must be covered by one of finitely many compatible color classes, paralleling ES’s finite residue covers and infinite certificate-line union.
why: The proof’s conflict-graph decomposition may suggest a systematic way to organize overlapping ES certificate lines without double-counting.
first_step: Map ES certificate families to vertices in a conflict graph (edges for incompatible residue coverage) and test whether a coloring gives a finite cover.

title: Group word-problem feature flip: equality versus existence
connection: Group word problems share ES’s finite words, matrix structure, and short certificates (F16w,F18,F32), but often ask whether two given words are equal, rather than whether some witness word exists. This feature flip marks a decision-versus-search distinction.
why: Normal-form methods help only if ES’s matrix semigroup has a usable normal form; testing this prevents conflating word equality with target reachability.
first_step: Check whether the ES generator set admits a normal form in SL₂(Z); if not, test the simpler congruence quotient search first.

title: Addition-chain recurrences as ES multiplicative closure analogues
connection: Addition chains share F02w,F16w,F30,F32: recursive operations extend certificates from known inputs, and special infinite families follow. ES also has multiple-closure and thin recursive prime families.
why: A recurrence on ES certificates might extend a solution at p to a controlled family of related primes or numerators.
first_step: Search the addition-chain constructions for an explicit certificate-extension recurrence and test whether an ES identity can realize n↦2n+c.

title: Universal Diophantine statements with multiplicative closure
connection: Universal representation problems share F01, F02, F06; multiplicative closure reduces the domain to primes plus local cases.
why: The reduction template may identify a clean prime-only theorem and prevent wasted effort on composite inputs.
first_step: Formalize the ES multiple-closure map and compare it with closure reductions in other universal Diophantine representation problems.

title: Local solubility without integral global points
connection: Local-global counterexamples share F06, F07, F27 and test whether local conditions suffice under positivity and integrality.
why: A catalogue of mechanisms helps distinguish a hidden obstruction from a genuinely hard global construction.
first_step: Compare ES with integral conic and norm-form examples having solutions at every completion but no integral point.

title: Exceptional primes for parametrised reciprocal identities
connection: Sparse algebraic failure sets share F08w, F25, F30, where a construction works except at explicit exceptional inputs.
why: A classification of failure sets may show that multiple parametrisations leave only a manageable intersection.
first_step: For each ES identity family, factor the obstruction polynomial and compare its prime roots with the failures of sister statements.

title: Lagrange's four squares: closure (Euler identity) + prime case by pigeonhole and descent — template for F02
connection: Four squares reduces to primes by a composition identity; the prime case is done by finding a multiple mp represented (pigeonhole) and descending m to 1. ES reduces to primes by trivial closure; the prime case has no descent.
why: An ES descent ('from a solution of a structured 4/(mp)-type equation produce one with smaller m') would be a Lagrange-type proof.
first_step: Search for an operation turning ES-type data at mp (e.g. a solution where m divides two of the denominators) into data at m'p with m' < m.

title: Feature flip F13 (cubic → quadric): 4/n = 1/x + 1/y is a hyperbola — fully solved by divisors
connection: The 2-term equation is a split conic; its solvability is a divisor-in-class condition and fails on a positive-density set. ES adds one variable and becomes a cubic surface with hyperbola fibres (F15).
why: Exactly measures what the extra dimension buys: from a single divisor condition (fails often) to a union over the fibre parameter (fails maybe never).
first_step: Compute the density of primes failing the 2-term condition for 4/p − 1/x as x ranges over the first K admissible values; plot the decay in K.

title: Feature flip F14: weighted equation 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 2/z is trivial — symmetry/unit numerators are load-bearing
connection: Trivial: x = y = z = p gives 1/p + 1/p + 2/p = 4/p. Also for p ≡ 1 (mod 4), x = (p+3)/4 leaves 12/(p(p+3)) = 3/N with N = p(p+3)/4, and 3/N = 1/N + 2/N. Breaking the unit-numerator symmetry kills the problem.
why: Confirms the difficulty sits in the symmetric unit-numerator structure (F12, F14) — any proof must use that all numerators are 1.
first_step: List all weightings (a,b,c) with a+b+c small for which a/x + b/y + c/z = 4/p is trivially solvable; the first non-trivial weighting is a sub-problem ladder.

title: Feature flip F24: sub-problems where the heuristic predicts infinitely many failures (single lines) — calibrate the union
connection: Each single ES line (e.g. (★) at a fixed level C) is expected to fail infinitely often (e.g. whenever 4Cp+1 is prime — infinitely often under Dickson/Schinzel); (★) overall fails at 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰; ES itself is verified to 10¹⁸.
why: The transition 'infinitely many failures → finitely many → none' along the union is a measurable phase diagram; its rate is the key heuristic input.
first_step: Plot, for unions of the first k lines (ordered by density), the count of failures ≤ X for X = 10⁶..10⁹; fit failure counts ~ X·exp(−c k).

title: Feature flip F38: Markoff (quadratic in each variable ⇒ Vieta group) vs ES (multilinear ⇒ no Vieta) — what symmetry group does the ES cubic have?
connection: The ES surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is multilinear; its automorphisms include S₃ and Cremona-type maps (x ↦ 1/x turns it into a plane 1/x+1/y+1/z linear in reciprocals!). In reciprocal coordinates X = 1/x it is the plane X + Y + Z = 4/n.
why: The integral-points problem is 'points of the plane X+Y+Z = 4/n with all coordinates unit fractions' — the symmetry group of the problem is the affine group of that plane preserving the unit-fraction lattice condition; a new angle on F38/F39.
first_step: Determine the group of birational automorphisms of the ES surface over ℚ that preserve positivity and integrality for infinitely many n.

title: Feature flip F03: n ≡ 0, 2, 3 mod 4 and non-square classes mod 840 are covered by identities — what if the hard classes were non-squares?
connection: Mordell's identities cover every class except the six square classes mod 840 (F03, F08, F09). The squares are exactly the classes no polynomial family can reach — the reciprocity obstruction is the reason.
why: Problems with a finite congruence covering of ALL classes are solved by identities; ES's residual set is forced to be the squares by reciprocity — the same reason as in Apollonian packings (HKRS).
first_step: For moduli M = 840·ℓ (ℓ ≤ 50), confirm the set of uncovered classes stays 'squares mod M' and record the minimal identity degree needed per class.

title: Feature flip F11 downward: 3/n = 1/x + 1/y fails for p ≡ 1 mod 3 — the 'numerator = terms + 1' ladder starts with a genuine obstruction
connection: 3/p as two unit fractions requires a divisor condition that fails for primes p ≡ 1 mod 3 (local-type obstruction), while 4/p in three terms has no local obstruction. m/n in m−1 terms: m = 3 fails, m = 4 is ES.
why: Shows ES is the first rung where the obstruction disappears; the reason (one extra free parameter) is quantifiable.
first_step: Verify the 3/p criterion and check m = 4 with 2 terms (4/p = 1/x + 1/y ⟺ p ≡ 3 mod 4) to complete the small ladder table.

title: Feature flip F36: problems where GRH IS known to give the pointwise result (least nonresidue, Artin, Ramanujan's form) — common structure
connection: Check whether in each GRH-success case (least nonresidue, Ramanujan's form x²+y²+10z², …) a single L-function or bounded family controls the event at the given n; caveat: Hooley's GRH proof of Artin uses infinitely many Kummer-field zeta functions and gives a density, so the criterion needs refinement. ES's event needs a family of size ≍ p of characters χ_{−4uB} at once.
why: Gives a structural criterion: count how many L-functions must be simultaneously controlled; ES needs too many for GRH-type explicit formulas.
first_step: For each GRH-success sibling, record the number of L-functions and the conductor range used; tabulate vs ES.

title: Feature flip F37: problems where a two-sided asymptotic for the pointwise count IS true (r₄(n) = 8σ*(n))
connection: Exact formulas (Jacobi) give two-sided control; ES provably has no two-sided polylog asymptotic (Linnik-type large values).
why: Confirms that ES requires a one-sided method; methods built on exact formulas (Jacobi-type) cannot be complete for ES.
first_step: List the exact formulae known for ES-like counts (theta-quotient normal form) and identify which term carries the Linnik large values.

title: Feature flip F27 (cone): 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x,y,z ∈ ℤ_{≠0} and at most one negative — count grows polynomially
connection: Allowing one negative denominator turns the problem into an indefinite one; check whether the solution count then grows like n^δ (it stays finite unless 4/n is a unit fraction). The positive cone cuts it down to polylog.
why: Counting solutions in sub-cones (e.g. one denominator 'barely negative') interpolates between trivial and ES; a continuity/sign-change argument across the cone boundary could be a route.
first_step: Count signed solutions with |negative denominator| ≤ p^θ for hard p and see how the count decays as θ → 0.

title: Pratt-certificate analogy: recursive ES certificates via factors of p-tied integers
connection: Pratt certificates for primality recurse on factors of p − 1. ES witnesses are divisors of p-tied integers (F10). A recursive scheme: a witness for p from 'witness-like data' for prime factors of 4Cp+1.
why: Recursive certificate structures sometimes reveal inductive proofs (as for Pratt: every prime has a short certificate, by induction).
first_step: For hard primes, record which prime factors q of 4Cp+1 'produce' the class −1 (q ≡ −1 mod 4C or products) and whether q's own ES data predict it.

title: Browning–Sofos–Teräväinen Bateman–Horn & polynomial Chowla with probability 1
connection: BST prove Bateman–Horn and polynomial Chowla for almost all polynomials in large families and deduce Hasse principle with probability 1 for families of varieties.
why: ES conditional results use Dickson/Bateman–Horn-type inputs (CONDITIONAL_ES.md); BST says such inputs hold for random polynomials.
first_step: List every polynomial whose Bateman–Horn behaviour would imply ES-type statements in CONDITIONAL_ES.md and check whether it lies in a BST family.
refs: Browning–Sofos–Teräväinen, Bateman–Horn, polynomial Chowla and the Hasse principle with probability 1, arXiv:2212.10373

title: Integer linear programming for minimal sterile residue systems
connection: Sterile residue classes (STERILE_*) are CRT systems where all certificates of bounded size fail; ILP can find minimal-modulus sterile systems or prove none exist below a bound.
why: Calibrates how deep sterility can go — the disproof-shape analogue of covering systems.
first_step: Encode 'class r mod M is sterile for all certificates with C ≤ K' as constraints and minimise M with an ILP solver for K ≤ 20.

title: OAI 026 positive lower density of large prime gaps (claimed) — calibration for sterile runs
connection: OAI 026 claims a positive proportion of prime gaps exceed C log p for any C; analogous 'long sterile runs' of slices at positive density would be a calibration point for ES heuristics.
why: Shows how 'rare-event at a fixed scale with positive density' results are proved — compare with ES's polylog windows.
first_step: Read the OAI 026 mechanism and test whether long failing slice-runs at fixed length have positive density among primes in data.

title: OAI 023 Patterson cubic Gauss sum first moment (claimed) — cubic analogue of ES characters
connection: OAI 023 claims Patterson's first-moment asymptotic unconditionally; ES's 'class of divisors' uses quadratic/Dirichlet characters, while 4/n ↔ cubic forms suggest cubic residue structure (cubic surface).
why: Low expectation; recorded because ES's cubic surface could have a cubic-character layer the campaign hasn't probed.
first_step: Test whether ES counts f(p) for p ≡ 1 (mod 3) correlate with the cubic residue character of 2 or 4 mod p.
refs: Dunn–Radziwiłł, Bias in cubic Gauss sums: Patterson's conjecture, arXiv:2109.07463

title: OAI 013 Ostmann inverse Goldbach (claimed) — additive irreducibility of ES-good sets
connection: OAI 013 claims the primes are not A+B up to finite modification; ES-type sets (n with Type I solution of a shape) have additive/multiplicative decomposition questions.
why: Not a route to ES, but a structural fact about sets of n defined by divisor events: the set of n covered by a family is a set of multiples (multiplicatively decomposable).
first_step: Record and close unless an additive decomposition of the covered set appears.

title: Littlewood–Offord in finite abelian groups (Juškevičius–Šemetulskis) — exact anti-concentration
connection: Sharp LO bounds in arbitrary abelian groups bound max_x P(Σ ε_i v_i = x) given that steps avoid small subgroups; ES needs a LOWER bound on P(= −1), the converse direction.
why: Clarifies that LO gives upper (anti-concentration) bounds; for ES a 'local limit theorem' (equidistribution of the walk) is needed — a different but standard tool.
first_step: Compute the local-limit error for the ±1/0 walk with ω ≈ log log N steps in (ℤ/e)^×; note the step count is far below the mixing time ~ log e.
refs: Juškevičius–Šemetulskis, Optimal Littlewood–Offord inequalities in groups, arXiv:1707.01085

title: Ramaré's local models / Ramaré–Walker for one-integer certificate densities
connection: Ramaré's local-model technique gives explicit lower bounds for sifted sums by matching local densities; the deep catalogue lists Ramaré–Walker as a thin-count precedent.
why: Template for explicit lower bounds with a small number of witnesses.
first_step: Re-read the deep catalogue entry and check whether ES's one-integer event fits Ramaré's 'local model' assumptions.
refs: Ramaré–Walker, Products of primes in arithmetic progressions: a footnote in parity breaking, J. Théor. Nombres Bordeaux 30 (2018)

title: Extreme-value prediction of ES's 'last hard prime' scale from sibling data
connection: Siblings with known last exceptions (I3: 2 433 600; U(n): 978145?) calibrate extreme-value models mapping expected count μ(n) to the largest failing n.
why: If the same model predicts ES's last failure below 2 (i.e. none), it quantifies P(ES false) consistently across siblings.
first_step: Fit log P(fail at n) ≈ −μ(n)·κ on siblings, then evaluate Σ_{p > 10^18} exp(−κ μ(p)).

title: Prehomogeneous vector space view: averages are easy, pointwise is the problem (calibration)
connection: Orbit-counting on prehomogeneous spaces gives averages over discriminants (Davenport–Heilbronn style). ES's averages are known (Vaughan, ET), and the pointwise question has no prehomogeneous analogue.
why: This calibrates what arithmetic statistics can give: possibly a positive-proportion statement in the n-aspect with explicit constants, not ES.
first_step: Skip unless a pointwise parametrisation arises. Note as a calibration entry.

title: Thue ratio set (signed): {u/v mod p : 0 < |u|, |v| ≤ √p} = F_p^*; ES₅ adds the divisibility uv | p + u + v
connection: By Thue's lemma every residue is u/v mod p with |u|, |v| ≤ √p, so the signed ratio set of small numbers covers all QNRs (with positive u, v only it can fail: p = 5 misses 4). Words use positive u, v. Words give A ≡ u/v (mod p) with the extra exact condition uv | p + u + v. ES₅ ⇔ some QNR has a Thue representation u/v satisfying the divisibility.
why: It isolates the divisibility condition as the entire content (the ratio set is already everything). Results on ratios u/v with arithmetic constraints, such as u, v smooth or prime (Shparlinski-type), are the native next step.
first_step: For p < 10⁶, count Thue pairs (u,v) of QNRs and the fraction satisfying uv | p + u + v; compare with the heuristic 1/(uv) per pair.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Goldbach exceptions are tied to one exceptional character — are ES/(★) failures tied to a character?
connection: In MV the only way to have many Goldbach exceptions is a Siegel zero. Analogue: (★)-failures (14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰) and b=1 failures (193, 2521, 66529) might share an extreme value of a single character statistic (e.g. least non-residue ℓ(p), or L(1, (·/p))).
why: If failures of sub-routes are 'explained' by one character, a Deuring–Heilbronn-type dichotomy becomes plausible.
first_step: For the 17 known sub-route failures and random controls compute ℓ(p), Σ_{m≤100}(m/p)/m, L(1,(·/p)) and the class number of Q(√p); compare ranks.

title: Powers-of-two slice: ES solutions with x = 2^k
connection: Goldbach–Linnik used the lacunary set of powers of 2. ES slice: 4/p = 1/2^k + 1/y + 1/z needs (2^{k+2} − p)/(p·2^k) to split into two unit fractions; e.g. via the divisor p it needs (2^{k+2} − p) | (2^i + 1) for some i ≤ k+2.
why: A lacunary, explicit family of candidate first denominators with rich multiplicative structure (2^i+1 factors via cyclotomy) — the ES analogue of Linnik's 2^v.
first_step: Compute, for p ≡ 1 (mod 24) up to 10⁷, the fraction of p having an ES solution with a power-of-2 denominator and the distribution of the least k.

title: Cauchy-lemma analogue: simultaneous control of (u+B, uB)
connection: Cauchy's lemma represents a number and its 'trace' simultaneously. (★) in pair form: s = u+B, q = uB with s ≡ −p (mod 4q) and s² − 4q a square. Seek an inequality region in (s,q) where existence is forced, as Cauchy's b² < 4a, 3a < b²+2b+4 does.
why: Simultaneous norm/trace representation is the mechanism behind every-n polygonal theorems; ES's (s,q) formulation is of the same shape (sum and product of two unknowns).
first_step: Plot, for many p, the set of (s,q) satisfying the congruence and check where the 'square discriminant' condition is hit; look for a region of guaranteed hits.
refs: Nathanson, Proc. AMS 99 (1987) 22-24 (A short proof of Cauchy's polygonal number theorem)

title: Furstenberg-set analogue: certificate 'lines' in the (C, d) plane
connection: Kakeya/Furstenberg estimates bound unions of lines/tubes from below. For fixed p, each prime q gives the 'line' {C ≡ c_q (mod q)} of levels where q | 4Cp+1; certificates are incidences of these lines with the conditions 4C | (product of chosen q's) + 1. An incidence-geometry lower bound might force a certificate.
why: Incidence bounds are robust every-configuration statements; ES at fixed p is an incidence problem between residue lines and divisibility conditions.
first_step: Plot, for small p, the incidence structure (q, c_q) and the certificate incidences; ask for the right incidence theorem (Szemerédi–Trotter over ℤ/q? Bourgain–Katz–Tao in F_q?).
refs: arXiv:2502.17655 (Wang-Zahl, Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions)

title: Power-size main terms are not enough: p + m² is open with a √n main term
connection: Hardy–Littlewood's conjecture that every large non-square n is p + m² has main term ≍ √n/log n, yet is open pointwise (binary). So 'lift ES to a count with a power-size main term' (TART items) is necessary but not sufficient: the lifted problem must also have enough free variables (ternary-or-more) for minor-arc control.
why: Self-correction for the power-main-term items: specifies the extra requirement (dimension) any lift must meet.
first_step: For each proposed lift V_p of ES, count the number of free variables after fixing p and compare with the Kloosterman/circle-method thresholds (≥ 4 for quadratic-type, more for cubic).
refs: Hardy-Littlewood, Partitio Numerorum III, Acta Math. 44 (1923) (Conjecture H)

title: The b=1 line as a 'Goldbach's other conjecture' model with sporadic failures
connection: The b=1 line fails at 193, 2521, 66529 and nowhere else ≤ 10¹¹ — like 5777 and 5993 for Goldbach's other conjecture. Fit the expected b=1 count at these primes and test whether failures are 'explained' by small expected counts; calibrate the same model on (★) (14 failures ≤ 10¹⁰).
why: Validates the heuristic models on sub-routes with real failures before trusting them for ES.
first_step: Compute the b=1 model main term at all p ≤ 10⁷ and the empirical P(fail | main term); check that the three failures sit at the extreme low end.

title: Non-vanishing on the line Re s = 1 analogue: a level Dirichlet series that cannot vanish
connection: PNT/Dirichlet need L(1 + it, χ) ≠ 0 via the 3-4-1 positivity trick (Mertens). For fixed p consider F_p(s) = Σ_C D_C(p) C^{−s} (finite sum): (★)(p) ⟺ F_p ≢ 0, and (★)(p) ⇒ ES(p) (not conversely: p = 409 fails (★) but satisfies ES). A '3-4-1'-type positivity combination of F_p, its twists, and F at related p might force non-vanishing.
why: Odd, but 3-4-1 is the archetype of extracting non-vanishing from positivity of a trigonometric polynomial.
first_step: Look for nonnegative trigonometric polynomials in a 'twist' variable (characters mod 4C) such that the combination of twisted level counts is ≥ c·(untwisted total) − (controlled).

title: Current-graph-style explicit constructions for one residue class mod a large modulus
connection: Ringel–Youngs used 'current graphs' — compact algebraic data generating a whole family. For one Mordell-hard class r mod M (M large, e.g. 840·1001), search for compact algebraic data (a finite list of certificate templates with parameters depending on p's residues mod M′) covering all primes in that class up to 10⁹.
why: Even if B1 forbids bounded templates for all p, the minimal template count per class reveals growth rates and hidden structure.
first_step: Run a greedy set-cover of primes in the class by parametric templates (Type II with C | M′) and plot template count vs X.

title: Landau–Siegel 'at most one exceptional modulus' analogue for ES levels
connection: Landau: at most one real character mod q ≤ Q has L(1,χ) tiny. ES analogue: among the characters χ_{−4uB} driving M_BM, show at most one (or boundedly many) can be 'exceptional' at p (strongly biased), so M_BM stays large except via one identifiable character whose effect can be handled separately.
why: The 'at most one exception' structure is what makes Siegel-type arguments work; ES's main term is a sum over many real characters.
first_step: Model T(p) as a sum over real characters and quantify how much a single character can reduce M_BM; compare with the observed minima of M_BM/L².

title: Stickiness analogue: certificates at nearby levels share prime factors
connection: Wang–Zahl handled 'sticky' Kakeya sets where tubes cluster coherently across scales. For fixed p, near-certificates at levels C and C + kq share the prime q (CRT); study whether certificate data are 'sticky' across levels (coherent families sharing primes) and whether non-sticky configurations are easier to force.
why: A structural dichotomy (sticky vs non-sticky) that may split the problem into two tractable halves.
first_step: Measure, for fixed p, the clustering of certificate-bearing levels modulo primes dividing their divisors.
refs: arXiv:2502.17655 (Wang-Zahl, Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions)
